A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAFE framework, three social-domain simulators, and F-MACEM use case. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite extensive rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation results, including intervention experiments, reward-term ablations, policy analyses, fairness–reward frontiers, and single-agent versus multi-agent learning comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains these original simulations and adds algorithm comparisons on full and simplified loan environments in Appendix D.6, plus runtime measurements in Appendix J.

M1.justification: The F-MACEM sampling and elite-update procedure and original simulator dynamics remain unchanged. However, v2 Appendix B inserts gamma^t discounting into reward and fairness aggregation that was undiscounted in v1 Equations 5–7, modestly revising the stated objective. Changed implementation or rerunning existing experiments is not established.

E1.justification: The original loan, healthcare, and education coverage is retained. Appendix D.6 adds MAFE-Loan-S, collapsing individuals' multistage trajectories into single decision events, creating a distinct simplified test scenario. New NCES/CDC mentions lack corresponding documentation establishing additional evaluated dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V1's fixed-policy and single-agent versus multi-agent comparisons are retained. V2 adds actual comparisons against fairness-augmented MAPPO and MADDPG, named F-MAPPO and F-MADDPG, on both full and simplified loan environments in Figure 11. This substantially broadens the algorithmic comparator set.

E3.justification: Appendix D.6 introduces a comparison allocating half the objective weight to profit and half to fairness, with step-wise training rewards for the policy-gradient baselines. The simplified condition changes observations, population size, feature dimensionality, episode length, and transition models. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original hyperparameter table's settings are retained.

E4.justification: The full-versus-simplified loan comparison adds a targeted diagnostic of whether learning difficulties arise from environmental complexity. Several factors change jointly. Existing intervention tests, reward-term ablations, learning-agent ablations, frontiers, and action analyses remain, often relocated to Appendix D.

E5.justification: V1 already displayed uncertainty bands and reported five intervention seeds and three frontier training seeds. V2 explicitly identifies shaded bands as standard deviations across seeds and reports runtime means and standard deviations in Table 9. No increase in the existing experiments' run counts is established.

E6.justification: Figure 11 adds the finding that F-MACEM substantially outperforms F-MAPPO and F-MADDPG on full MAFE-Loan, while all three learn in the simplified environment. Table 9 newly reports average step costs of 0.13 seconds for Loan, 0.25 for Health, and 0.40 for Edu. These extend the result set; earlier findings are largely retained rather than improved under matched settings.

T1.justification: V2 adds discounting to the formal aggregation definitions and omits v1's general constrained-to-regularized optimization formulation while retaining the cooperative objective. Its healthcare example changes the mortality denominator from ended illnesses to population, although Appendix G retains the former definition. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains three MAFE testbeds for dynamic multi-agent fairness. V2 adds explicit open-source and reproducibility claims and calls MAFE the first permutation-equivariant environment in Section 4; v1 described permutation equivariance as a design requirement without this priority claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting algorithm performance to exploration strategy, temporal aggregation, and environmental complexity. It explicitly identifies cooperative-only evaluation as a limitation and adds cautions about fairness-metric misuse and domain validation in Sections 7–8. The earlier realism caveat and coordination interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-release URL absent from v1 and adds two-layer MLP details, CPU specifications, training duration, step and update costs, and construction details for the simplified environment. These substantially expand access and execution information, although baseline training details remain incomplete and Table 8 retains obsolete equation references.

R1.justification: V2 adds MARL-fairness references, including Zimmer, Grupen, Ju, Wong, and Aloor, and citations to alternative CEM formulations. It sharpens the distinction between population-level and agent-level fairness and adds a permutation-equivariance novelty claim. The broader positioning around heterogeneous, realistic, multidomain environments remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and framework exposition are extensively rewritten. V2 reorganizes contributions and environment descriptions, foregrounds healthcare in the main experiments, moves detailed metric definitions and broader analyses into the appendix, promotes the algorithm into the main text, and adds an appendix contents page and impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 splits and revises the introductory illustrations, reorganizes main-text plots around healthcare, and relocates and reformats the multidomain figures. It adds a metric-summary table, algorithm-comparison figure, and runtime table. The appendix changes from two-column to single-column layout, substantially altering figure, table, and text presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 offers clearer organization, useful conventional MARL comparisons, and substantially better code-access and computational information. The gains are limited by jointly changed factors in the simplified experiment, incomplete baseline settings, inconsistent healthcare metric definitions, and stale hyperparameter cross-references. With the original contribution and most evidence retained, the net quality improvement is limited.
